glossary.Dyspnoea: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.
glossary.Palpitations: An awareness of your own heartbeat, often fast, strong or irregular.
glossary.Hoarseness: A rough, weak or croaky voice, often from a problem with the vocal cords or their nerve.
glossary.S1: The first heart sound, made by the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole.
glossary.P2: The pulmonary valve part of the second heart sound; loud when pulmonary pressure is high.
glossary.Apex: The tip of the heart, felt in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
glossary.Regurgitation: Backward leak of blood through a valve that does not close properly.
glossary.Stenosis: Abnormal narrowing of a valve or vessel.
glossary.Diastole: The phase of the heartbeat when the ventricles relax and fill with blood.
glossary.Systole: The phase of the heartbeat when the ventricles contract and pump blood out.
glossary.LA: Left atrium, the chamber receiving blood from the lungs before it passes to the left ventricle.
glossary.LV: Left ventricle, the main pumping chamber that sends blood to the body.
glossary.Left atrium: The heart chamber that receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
glossary.Left ventricle: The thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta.
glossary.Streptococcal: Caused by Streptococcus bacteria, such as the group A strep that causes sore throats.
glossary.Infective endocarditis: Infection of the heart valves or inner heart lining, usually by bacteria.
glossary.MI: Myocardial infarction: death of heart muscle from a blocked coronary artery (a heart attack).
glossary.Inferior MI: A heart attack affecting the bottom wall of the heart, usually from a blocked right coronary artery.
glossary.Pulmonary venous pressure: The pressure in the veins draining the lungs into the left atrium.
glossary.Beta-blocker: A drug such as bisoprolol that slows the heart and reduces its workload.
glossary.Enalapril: An ACE inhibitor used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
glossary.Rate control: Slowing the heart rate in AF without trying to restore normal rhythm.
glossary.Rhythm control: Treatment that aims to restore and keep normal sinus rhythm in AF.
glossary.Stroke: Brain damage from a blocked or burst blood vessel; AF clots can travel to the brain.
glossary.Valvuloplasty: Widening a narrowed valve, usually with a balloon passed through a vein.
glossary.Commissurotomy: Splitting the fused edges (commissures) of valve leaflets to widen the valve.
glossary.Percutaneous: Done through the skin with a needle or catheter rather than open surgery.
glossary.Valve replacement: Surgery that removes a diseased valve and fits a mechanical or tissue valve.
glossary.LV dysfunction: Weak or impaired pumping of the left ventricle.
glossary.Calcification: Build-up of calcium deposits that stiffen tissue such as valve leaflets.
glossary.Cardiogenic shock: Dangerously low blood pressure and organ perfusion because the heart cannot pump enough.
glossary.RCA: Right coronary artery, which usually supplies the inferior wall of the heart.
glossary.Autoimmune: When the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.
glossary.Antigen: A molecule that the immune system recognises and responds to.
glossary.Incompetent valve: A valve that does not close fully, so blood leaks backwards.
glossary.Volume overload: A heart chamber having to handle more blood than normal, which stretches it over time.
glossary.Heart failure: The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, causing breathlessness and fluid build-up.
glossary.Diuretic: A drug that makes the kidneys pass more salt and water, relieving fluid overload.
glossary.Fluid overload: Too much fluid in the body, causing swollen legs and fluid in the lungs.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity.
glossary.Gold standard: The best available test or treatment against which others are judged.
